# ARTH — BUILD SPECIFICATION

**From:** Director, Product Engineering
**To:** Development team, Advito Global · IT Director · cc Prem Kumar
**Date:** 21 August 2026
**Version:** 1.0 — supersedes the front-end handover of 18 August for anything the two disagree on
**Companion:** `Arth-Platform.html` — 80 screens, 22 seats, opens in any browser

---

## §0 WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES AND DOES NOT DO

**It does:** name every object, every state and every transition; give each of the 80 screens a route, a landing seat, an access list, its outbound navigation and its actions; state what happens after each action; and give a build order in dependency sequence.

**It does not make the build error-free, and no document can.** A specification that claims to is dangerous, because people stop asking questions. **What this removes is guessing.** Where something here is wrong or expensive, raise it — that is a conversation, not a deviation.

**Three categories, unchanged from the handover.** Binding: §1 to §4. Illustrative: every name, number and pixel in the prototype. Not costed: anything whose data does not exist, listed in §7.

**One standing rule.** Where this document and the prototype disagree, **this document wins.** Where this document is silent, the prototype is the reference. Where both are silent, ask rather than choose.

---

## §1 THE OBJECT MODEL

Fifteen objects. Everything else is derived.

### Identity and structure

| Object | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Tenant` | A dealer group | Isolation enforced by row-level security, not application code |
| `Brand` | Arena, Nexa, a second manufacturer | Sits **between** group and branch |
| `Branch` | A rooftop | Working hours live here |
| `Position` | A named post in the org tree | **Step owners and escalation targets are Positions, never Users** |
| `User` | A person, and their seat | Carries `workspaceKey` — the one screen they land on |

### The customer side

| Object | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Customer` | One person | **Shared across every department.** Never duplicated per module |
| `Household` | A group of customers at one address | Phase 6. Slot exists earlier, weak line inside it |
| `Vehicle` | One car, by registration and chassis | Shared. Service, sales and insurance all write to it |
| `Consent` | Purpose, channel, captured-at, source | **One row per purpose.** Never one tick for everything |

### The work

| Object | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `Lead` | One enquiry | Current state only. History lives in the ledger |
| `LeadEvent` | Append-only ledger of everything that happened | Same transaction as the `Lead` write |
| `Quotation` | A priced offer | **Freezes the price and scheme versions live at that moment** |
| `Booking` | A committed sale | Carries value in paise. **Carries no delivery date** — see below |
| `DeliveryPromise` | Append-only ledger of promised dates | **New. The current promise is the latest row** |
| `DeliveryChain` / `ChainStep` | The steps, their owners, their SLAs | Steps are **rows, not code** |
| `JobCard` | A service visit | Phase 5 |
| `Policy` | Insurance, warranty, RSA, AMC | Phase 5 |
| `Case` | A complaint | Phase 5 |
| `ExceptionEvent` | Append-only ledger of cockpit decisions | DDL issued. Deferred by ruling |

### Derived, never stored

Storing any of these creates a value that can drift from the thing it describes.

| Derived | From |
|---|---|
| Current delivery promise | Latest `DeliveryPromise` row |
| Chain state, chain age | Walk of `ChainStep` states |
| Exception state | Latest `ExceptionEvent` for the identity |
| **Parked** | Latest disposition is `POSTPONED` **and** revisit date is in the future |
| Lead difficulty band | Computed at assignment, then **frozen** — the one exception, and it is frozen because it must not move |
| Expected value | §5 |

---

## §2 STATE MACHINES

### 2.1 Lead — nine stages

```
New → Assigned → Contacted → Qualified → Test drive
    → Quotation → Negotiation → Booked → Delivered
```

**Rules:**

- Stages are **tenant configuration**. The nine are the default, not a constant.
- **Forward by any amount. Backward only by a manager, with a reason, and it writes a `LeadEvent`.**
- After `Booked`, progress is the delivery chain's to report. The lead reads `Booked` until a car is handed over. **Do not mirror chain steps as stages.**
- `Lost` is terminal and requires a reason from the controlled list. **Never free text.**
- `Parked` is not a stage. It is derived.
- A lead may carry a delivered car and still read open — a second vehicle on the same enquiry.

### 2.2 Disposition — what a contact produces

Every call ends in exactly one outcome. **No outcome, no save.** Full table in the prototype's `disp` screen; the rules that govern all of them:

| Rule | |
|---|---|
| Connection under 20 seconds | Counts as not connected. **No points, no penalty** |
| Points | `base × difficulty multiplier`. Multiplier hidden from the executive |
| Promise typed after a call | Becomes a tracked commitment with a deadline |
| `POSTPONED` | **Requires a revisit date.** Lead stays open, reads Parked |
| `LOST` | Requires a reason, and each reason demands a specific fact |
| Callback beyond 14 days | Requires a reason |
| Every outcome | Writes a `LeadEvent`. Nothing is edited |

### 2.3 Delivery chain

Three lanes in parallel: **finance and insurance · vehicle and registration · preparation**. Twelve steps by default; EV adds two, commercial vehicle adds three, two-wheeler removes one. **All of it seed data.**

- The promised date is the **longest path**, recomputed on every step change, and **written as a new `DeliveryPromise` row each time it moves.**
- A step is `PENDING · IN_PROGRESS · BLOCKED · COMPLETE`.
- `BLOCKED` carries a reason **and a kind: internal or external.**
- **External blocks are excluded from promise accuracy, and the exclusion is itself reported.** A branch marking everything external must be visible.
- A salesperson may override a computed date. The override is recorded with a reason. **A date typed with nothing behind it must not be possible.**

### 2.4 Exception — deferred by ruling

`ExceptionEvent` is append-only. Four events, five constraints, four return triggers, one hard restriction: **a walk-up card cannot be acknowledged again.** DDL is issued and awaiting Prem. **Not in this cycle.**

---

## §3 ACCESS — THE THREE LAYERS

They are separate and they are commonly confused.

| Layer | Question | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **Landing** | Where does this person start? | `User.workspaceKey`. Exactly one, never a list |
| **Permission** | What may this person open? | Role grants, per screen |
| **Scope** | Which records within it? | Own / team / branch / brand / group |

**A branch manager lands on his decisions screen and can still reach telecalling. Landing is not permission.**

### 3.1 The two rules that govern every seat

1. **No seat opens another department's workspace.** If a service advisor needs one fact from sales, sales sends him that fact. He is never given the sales screen.
2. **Information flows out of service, never in.** An advisor flags an exchange interest; sales, used car and central telecalling see a potential lead. He never sees the pipeline, the model, the value, or who is handling it.

### 3.2 Figures, by seat

| Figure | Executive | Team leader | Branch head | Principal | Dealer admin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Own records | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Colleagues' records | See only | Team | Branch | All | All |
| Lead cost by source | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Lead difficulty band** | **No** | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Discount given | Own | Team | Branch | All | All |
| **Insurance / product margin** | **No** | **No** | **No** | **No** | **Yes** |
| Branch P&L | No | No | Own | All | No |
| Salary and employee cost | No | No | No | Yes | No |
| **What the dealer pays Advito** | No | No | No | Yes | **Yes** |
| Export | **No** | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |

**Two rows are not configurable:** salary is never visible below the principal, and margin is dealer-admin only. Everything else the dealer may adjust.

### 3.3 Advito-side

Three surfaces, not one panel. **Recorded as unscoped — it needs its own work order and is not in this cycle.** When it comes: Master sees pricing and margin; Support can fix configuration, sees masked phone numbers, no pricing, and **every entry is logged and shown to the dealer**; Engineering sees health and errors and no customer data in the clear.

---

## §4 CROSS-CUTTING RULES

These apply to every screen and are the ones most often lost.

**The standard row.** Nine columns, one grid, every department. Columns 1, 5, 6, 8, 9 never change. **Every date carries the event that produced it** — *"Call, no answer · 03 Aug"*, never a bare date.

**After an action.** The panel becomes the confirmation **in place**, for about 1.5 seconds: what was recorded, what it earned, what happens next. **Not a toast** — at forty times a morning a toast is chrome. **Undo inside that window**, implemented as a correcting entry, never a deletion.

**Save.** Every form ends in a save bar. A persistent unsaved-changes bar appears on first edit and clears on save or navigate.

**Empty, error, offline.** States a fact and says what happens next. Names the person who can grant access when refused. Work is never blocked offline; the queue syncs.

**Partial data.** An incomplete figure says so beside itself. **An incomplete number rendered as final is the fastest way to lose a dealer.**

**Colour.** Every value resolves to a token. Zero raw hexes. Five button variants and **no green button.** Semantic colour never decorates.

**Free text or controlled list.** *Will anybody ever put this field in a `GROUP BY`?* Yes → list. No → free text.

**Working hours gate every clock.** Nothing outside a branch's hours creates a penalty. A lead arriving at 21:40 starts its clock next working morning, and the delay is recorded against the branch.

---

## §5 THE FORMULAS

**Expected value**

```
expected value = (unit gross + attached gross) × stage probability
```

`unit gross` from the price master. `attached gross` = exchange + finance + insurance + accessories, **each at its own attach rate for that model at that dealership**, average case not best case. `stage probability` = historical conversion from that stage to a delivered car, cut by source.

**At launch there is no history.** Start from a seeded default table, replace with the dealer's own numbers after month one, and **mark the figure provisional until then.**

**Points**

```
points = base(outcome) × difficulty multiplier(band)
```

Bands ×1.0 / ×1.5 / ×2.5 / ×3.5, dealer-configurable. **System-computed at assignment, then frozen.** Hidden from the executive.

**Cost per booking** — marketing spend ÷ bookings, per source, **exact where an API reports it and manually entered where it does not.** Never merged with total cost per booking, which adds salaries and rent and is directional only.

**Promise accuracy** — delivered on or before the promise ÷ all deliveries, **excluding externally blocked chains**, with the exclusion count reported alongside.

## APPENDIX B — EVERY SCREEN

**Derived from the prototype, not written from memory.** `Reached by` is the definitive access list. `Navigates to` is the outbound link map — build these and no screen is a dead end.


### Sales and telecalling


**`dayb` · Today  the day panel** — *Screen B. One panel, three readings*  
Route `/w/dayb` · Reached by: `tele`  
Navigates to: `tele`  

**`recep` · Front desk** — *Receptionist, arrivals and calls*  
Route `/w/recep` · Reached by: `recep`  
Navigates to: `walkin`  
Primary actions: Log a walk in · Answer

**`lead` · Team leader** — *Approvals, unassigned, coaching*  
Route `/w/lead` · Reached by: `lead`  
Navigates to: `discount`, `targets`  
Primary actions: Weekly review

**`discount` · Discount request** — *Written justification on the record*  
Route `/w/discount` · Reached by: `lead`  
Navigates to: `quote`  
Primary actions: Send for approval · Save draft · Cancel

**`fni` · Finance and insurance desk** — *Files, financier performance*  
Route `/w/fni` · Reached by: `fni`  
Primary actions: New file

**`tele` · Call queue** — *The floor, with anti-gaming rules*  
Route `/w/tele` · Reached by: `mgr`, `svctele`, `tele`

<section id="s1">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 01</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>What Arth is</h2>
  <p class="lede2">Arth is the system that makes a car dealership answerable for every enquiry it receives, every promise it makes, and every rupee it spends winning a customer.</p>

  <p>A dealer group buys advertising, receives enquiries, works them across several departments, sells cars, services them, renews their insurance, and takes them back in part exchange. Today each of those steps lives in a different system or in no system at all, and <b>nobody in the building can answer the two questions that matter most: what happened to that enquiry, and what did that customer cost us.</b></p>

  <p>Arth answers both, and it answers them with evidence rather than assertion.</p>

  <div class="pull">Every enquiry has an owner and a clock. Every promise has a name against it. Every rupee of advertising can be traced to a delivered car.</div>

  <h3>The name</h3>
  <p><b>अर्थ</b> is one of the four Puruṣārthas: purpose, and wealth legitimately earned. Both meanings are load-bearing. The product exists to give a dealership's activity a purpose it can see, and to make the money it earns traceable to the work that earned it.</p>

  <p>The mark is the word <em>arth</em> in lowercase, hanging from a brass rule. Devanagari hangs its letters from a line; an accounting ledger rules a line before a total. <b>We overline where everyone else underlines.</b></p>

  <h3>The one-sentence test</h3>
  <p>If a dealer principal asks what this is, the answer is not <em>a CRM</em>. It is:</p>
  <div class="dark"><span class="eyebrow">The answer</span>
    <b>"It is the system that tells you which enquiries nobody called, which promises you broke, and which advertising actually sold a car."</b><br><br>
    Every one of those three is a thing he currently cannot find out, and every one of them costs him money this month.</div>
</section>

<!-- 02 -->
<section id="s2">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 02</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The problem, evidenced</h2>
  <p class="lede2">These are not hypotheses. Each one was measured on a live dealer group during the build.</p>

  <div class="stat">
    <div><div class="v">440</div><div class="l">Enquiries in one month that were never contacted at all</div></div>
    <div><div class="v">₹38,000</div><div class="l">Spent on a campaign that produced the cheapest leads and not one car</div></div>
    <div><div class="v">78%</div><div class="l">Of service promises met, against a target of 90</div></div>
    <div><div class="v">0</div><div class="l">Recorded reasons for the 419 enquiries closed as lost</div></div>
  </div>

  <h3>The five failures</h3>

  <h4>1 · The enquiry nobody called</h4>
  <p>A quarter of enquiries at a typical group are never contacted. Not badly contacted. <b>Never contacted.</b> They arrive after hours, or during a shift change, or they are assigned to somebody on leave, and no mechanism notices. At an average margin per model, 440 uncontacted enquiries is roughly <b>₹39 lakh of business that never had a conversation.</b></p>

  <h4>2 · The lead cost that means nothing</h4>
  <p>Every dealer knows his cost per lead. Almost none knows his cost per booking, and the two point in opposite directions. In the month we measured, the campaign with the <b>cheapest leads in the entire portfolio at ₹165 produced zero cars.</b> On a cost-per-lead report it was the best campaign of the month.</p>

  <h4>3 · The promise nobody owns</h4>
  <p>A delivery date is agreed verbally, typed into nothing, and broken. The customer finds out on the day. Nobody can say who promised it or when it moved, because <b>the date is a field that holds only its current value.</b></p>

  <h4>4 · The disposition that is a lie</h4>
  <p>Before the anti-gaming rules, <em>not interested</em> ran at 31% of all dispositions at this group, almost none of it with a reason. A telecaller protecting his conversion rate marks hard leads dead. <b>The dealership never learns why it loses, because the reason was never recorded and cannot be reconstructed.</b></p>

  <h4>5 · The department that cannot see the customer</h4>
  <p>A service advisor has a customer's car on the lift whose insurance expires in six weeks, whose household has an open enquiry for a new vehicle, and whose service history would settle an exchange valuation to within 3%. He can see none of it, because service, sales and insurance keep separate records of the same person.</p>

  <div class="note"><b>The common thread:</b> none of these is a discipline problem, and none is solved by telling people to try harder. Each is a system that cannot see something, and each becomes visible the moment one record is shared and one ledger is kept.</div>
</section>

  <div class="warn"><b>The buyer and the heaviest user are different people, and the product has to satisfy both.</b> A dealer principal who loves it and a floor that will not use it produces a cancelled contract in month four. Every screen is designed for the person in front of it, which is why a telecaller's day looks nothing like a principal's.</div>
</section>

<!-- 04 -->
<section id="s4">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 04</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>What Arth is not</h2>
  <p class="lede2">A product is defined as much by its refusals. Each of these was considered and declined for a stated reason.</p>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="card"><h5>Not a CRM</h5><p>Every dealer has one and it changed nothing. A CRM stores contacts. Arth enforces accountability, which is a different job with a different measure of success.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Not a DMS</h5><p>The manufacturer mandates one and it handles inventory, invoicing and warranty. Competing with it is a five-year build against an incumbent the dealer cannot remove.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Not a dashboard</h5><p>A dashboard reports. It shows a number and stops. Arth surfaces decisions, and a card that has no action is a report and belongs in a table.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Not a marketing tool</h5><p>It does not create campaigns or design creative. It measures which of them sold a car, which is a harder and more valuable thing.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Not an HR system</h5><p>It computes what an incentive should be and exports it. It never pays anybody, never touches a bank account, never holds a salary.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Not a telephony platform</h5><p>It integrates with one. Building call infrastructure is a licensed business with its own regulator.</p></div>
  </div>

  <div class="pull">A product that refuses nothing has no shape, and a product with no shape cannot be sold in a sentence.</div>
</section>

<!-- 05 -->
<section id="s5">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 05</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The competitive picture</h2>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Who</th><th>What they are</th><th>Why a dealer still has the problem</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>AUTOSherpa, Groweon</b></td><td>Indian automotive CRMs</td>
      <td>Lead capture and follow-up. No spend data, so cost per booking cannot exist</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Salesforce, LeadSquared</b></td><td>Horizontal CRMs</td>
      <td>Configurable into anything, which means a dealer pays a consultant to invent a dealership</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>CDK, Excellon</b></td><td>Dealer management systems</td>
      <td>Excellent at inventory and invoicing. The enquiry is the last thing they model</td></tr>

      <td>The strongest architecture in the category, and the right principle, one shared data core. Priced and scoped for large groups</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Spyne and similar</b></td><td>AI point tools</td>
      <td>Solve one narrow task well. Not a system of record</td></tr>
  </table>

  <div class="dark"><span class="eyebrow">The gap nobody occupies</span>
    Every product above sits on one side of a line. <b>CRMs know what the dealership did. Ad platforms know what was spent. Nothing holds both.</b><br><br>
    So no dealer in India can answer <em>what did this delivered car cost me to win</em>, and that is the question the person paying the bill actually has.</div>
</section>

<!-- 06 -->
<section id="s6">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 06</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The moat</h2>
  <p class="lede2">Arth has exactly one defensible advantage, and it is not the software.</p>

  <div class="pull">Advito is the dealer's media buyer. Ad spend and delivered cars sit in the same database because the same company controls both ends.</div>

  <p>A software vendor can ask a dealer for read access to his Meta account. Some will grant it, most will not, and none will grant the granular creative-level spend needed to compute cost per booking by advert. <b>We do not ask, because we are already inside the ad account. We placed the spend.</b></p>

  <h3>What this makes possible that competitors cannot copy</h3>
  <ul>
    <li><b>Cost per booking by creative</b>, not merely by campaign, which tells a dealer what to stop making, rather than where to spend more.</li>
    <li><b>Delivered cars fed back to the platforms</b> as conversion events, so the same budget bids better. We do not only measure the spend; we improve it.</li>
    <li><b>Two-year source value.</b> Portal leads cost more to win and are worth less afterwards: fewer services, lower renewal rates. Computing that needs the same customer record two years later and the original spend figure.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="note"><b>The strategic consequence:</b> Arth is worth most to a dealer whose advertising we also run, and worth least to one who buys the software alone. <b>That is a feature, not a limitation.</b> It makes the agency relationship stickier than either product alone, and it is why the two are sold together.</div>

  <h4>The honest weakness</h4>
  <p>The moat is commercial, not technical. Another agency in another city could do the same thing. <b>What protects us is being first in this segment with a built product, and the switching cost of a dealership's two years of history living in our database.</b></p>
</section>

<!-- 07 -->
<section id="s7">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 07</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The eleven principles</h2>
  <p class="lede2">These settle arguments. When a decision is contested, it is resolved against this list rather than by seniority.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th style="width:30px"></th><th>Principle</th><th>What it rules out</th></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">01</td><td><b>One shared record</b><br>One Customer, one Vehicle, one Household</td><td>Any module keeping its own copy of a person</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">02</td><td><b>Ownership attaches to activities, never to the customer</b></td><td>A salesperson "owning" a household for life</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">03</td><td><b>Nothing is edited. A correction is a new entry</b></td><td>Any screen that lets history be rewritten</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">04</td><td><b>Every number carries its source and period</b></td><td>A bare figure with nothing behind it</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">05</td><td><b>A card with no action is a report</b></td><td>Dashboards presented as decisions</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">06</td><td><b>Silence when nothing is wrong</b></td><td>Notifications that train people to ignore them</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">07</td><td><b>Points measure behaviour, targets measure outcome, and they never merge</b></td><td>One score that gets gamed within six weeks</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">08</td><td><b>Hard leads are worth more than easy ones</b></td><td>Cherry-picking the hot list</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">09</td><td><b>No role opens another department's workspace</b></td><td>A service advisor browsing the sales pipeline</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">10</td><td><b>Fail toward visibility</b><br>On any doubt, show it</td><td>A suppression that quietly hides money</td></tr>
    <tr><td class="rt">11</td><td><b>A threshold about human behaviour is set from real behaviour</b></td><td>Numbers invented in advance and defended later</td></tr>
  </table>

  <div class="dark"><span class="eyebrow">Two standing tests</span>
    <b>A safeguard whose safe path does not exist is a pressure, not a safeguard.</b> If a rule leaves somebody no legitimate way out, they will find an illegitimate one.<br><br>
    <b>Will anybody ever put this field in a GROUP BY?</b> If yes it is a controlled list. If no it is free text. That single question settles every field-type argument.</div>
</section>

<section id="s8">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 08</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The seven workspaces</h2>
  <p class="lede2">A workspace is a department's day. Eighty screens across twenty-two seats, and every one of them belongs to one of these seven.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Workspace</th><th>The job</th><th>The measure that matters</th><th>State</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Telecalling</b></td><td>Work a finite queue of enquiries to an outcome</td><td>First response time · connect rate · weighted points</td><td><span class="pill p-ok">Built</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Sales</b></td><td>Move an enquiry through nine stages to a booking</td><td>Cost per booking · stage conversion</td><td><span class="pill p-ok">Built</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Delivery</b></td><td>Booking to handover across three parallel lanes</td><td>Promise accuracy</td><td><span class="pill p-mid">In build</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Service</b></td><td>Job cards against promised times</td><td>Revenue per bay-hour · retention</td><td><span class="pill p-mute">Phase 5</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Insurance and renewals</b></td><td>Insurance, warranty, RSA and AMC by expiry</td><td>Renewal conversion · lapse recovery</td><td><span class="pill p-mute">Phase 5</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Used car</b></td><td>Valuation, stock and retail</td><td>Gross per unit · days in stock</td><td><span class="pill p-mute">Phase 5</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Management</b></td><td>Decisions, money, and comparison across branches</td><td>The seven to nine things that need a person today</td><td><span class="pill p-mid">Partial</span></td></tr>
  </table>

  <h3>Three cross-cutting layers</h3>
  <p>These are not workspaces. They run underneath all seven and are what make the product one system rather than seven.</p>
  <div class="grid">
    <div class="card"><h5>The record layer</h5><p>Customer, Household, Vehicle, Documents. Shared by every department, which is why a service advisor can see a renewal and an evaluator can price an exchange to 3%.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>The accountability layer</h5><p>The ledger, the clocks, the points, the difficulty weighting, the escalation ladders. Chapter 09.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>The money layer</h5><p>Attribution, cost per booking, source investment, discount leakage, incentives. Chapter 11.</p></div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- 09 -->
<section id="s9">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 09</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The accountability layer</h2>
  <p class="lede2">This is the product. Everything else is a workspace that writes to it.</p>

  <h3>The ledger</h3>
  <p>Every meaningful event writes an append-only row: assignment, call attempt, outcome, commitment, stage change, price change, approval, export. <b>Nothing can be edited or deleted, at the database level rather than by convention.</b> Update and delete privileges are revoked from the application role entirely.</p>
  <p>This is what makes Arth usable as evidence in a payout dispute or a disciplinary matter. An editable record is worth nothing in either.</p>

  <h3>The clock</h3>
  <p>Every enquiry carries a first-response target and every promise carries a deadline. <b>Working hours gate all of it.</b> A lead arriving at 21:40 starts its clock the next working morning, and the delay is recorded against the branch rather than the executive, because penalising a person for being asleep is how a floor learns to distrust a system in its first week.</p>

  <h3>The anti-gaming rules</h3>
  <p>Any scoring system will be gamed. These exist because the specific ways are predictable.</p>
  <table>
    <tr><th>The move</th><th>What stops it</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Dial and hang up to inflate call count</td><td>Under 20 seconds counts as not connected. No points, and no penalty either</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Mark hard leads dead to protect a conversion rate</td><td>Every closure demands a specific fact, checked against the recording. Repeated closures are flagged</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Cherry-pick the hot list</td><td>Difficulty weighting. A cold lead is worth 2.5× a hot one</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Inflate a subordinate's difficulty band</td><td>System-computed, never manager-set, and frozen at assignment</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Waive penalties selectively for favourites</td><td>Every waiver is recorded with a reason and counted against the manager who granted it</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Keep a dead lead alive on paper</td><td>A callback beyond 14 days requires a reason</td></tr>
  </table>

  <div class="dark"><span class="eyebrow">The insight behind difficulty weighting</span>
    On raw points, the executive who takes only easy leads is the best performer on the floor. <b>Weighted for how hard his leads were, he is the worst.</b><br><br>
    One dealership's figures: Executive B scored 448 raw and 512 weighted. Executive C scored 386 raw and <b>802 weighted</b>. C had looked mediocre for a year.</div>

  <h3>The escalation ladder</h3>
  <p>Four rungs, every one configurable: executive → team leader at 2 hours → branch head at 6 → dealer principal at 24, <b>with a rupee value attached at the top rung</b>, because that is what makes a principal act rather than note.</p>
</section>

<!-- 10 -->
<section id="s10">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 10</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The delivery chain</h2>
  <p class="lede2">The gap nobody has filled. Every competitor's product stops at the booking, and the booking is where the customer's experience actually begins.</p>

  <p>Between a signature and a handover sit twelve steps across three departments, three lanes running in parallel, and four external parties nobody in the dealership controls. <b>The delivery date is the longest path through it</b>, recomputed whenever any step moves.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Lane</th><th>Steps</th><th>Blocked by</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Finance and insurance</b></td><td>File submitted · sanction · disbursement · policy</td><td>The customer's documents, then the bank</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Vehicle and registration</b></td><td>Allocated · dispatched · received · registered</td><td>The manufacturer, transport, the RTO</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Preparation</b></td><td>Accessories ordered · fitted · pre-delivery check · handover</td><td>Stock and bay capacity, both ours</td></tr>
  </table>

  <h3>The two rules that make it work</h3>
  <p><b>The promised date is an event, never a field.</b> Every movement writes a new row. Without this, three things are permanently impossible: counting how often a promise moved, measuring promise accuracy against what was promised at booking, and answering the most-asked question in any delivery dispute: <em>who told the customer the 12th?</em></p>

  <p><b>Internal and external blocks are different things.</b> An RTO strike is not the branch's fault and must be excluded from its promise accuracy, or the metric is worthless and the branch stops believing every other number too. <b>But the exclusion is itself reported</b>, so a branch marking everything external is visible.</p>

  <h3>What the customer sees</h3>
  <p>One page, no login, a signed link that expires at delivery plus thirty days. It names a human. <b>It never shows an internal step name and never hides a slip.</b> Telling a customer the truth on the 14th is survivable; his discovering it on the 18th is not.</p>

  <div class="note"><b>Commercially, this is the referral engine.</b> A dealer principal who can show this page to another dealer principal has done our selling for us, and status messages are WhatsApp <em>utility</em> messages, roughly seven times cheaper than marketing messages. Getting that classification right is worth lakhs a year at scale.</div>
</section>

<!-- 11 -->
<section id="s11">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 11</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>The money layer</h2>
  <p class="lede2">The chapter that justifies the invoice.</p>

  <h3>Every source on one basis</h3>
  <p>Ad platforms report themselves. Everything else has to be entered, and <b>if it is not entered it looks free</b>, which is how showroom rent and event budgets escape scrutiny for years. Arth costs all of them on the same basis.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Source</th><th>How the cost is known</th><th class="rt">Cost per lead</th><th class="rt">Cost per booking</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Meta, Festive C2</td><td>Exact, ad account</td><td class="rt">₹412</td><td class="rt">₹9,200</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Meta, Festive C3</td><td>Exact, ad account</td><td class="rt">₹165</td><td class="rt" style="color:var(--over)">no bookings</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Service walk-in, upgrade</td><td>Retention spend apportioned</td><td class="rt">₹500</td><td class="rt" style="color:var(--set)">₹2,200</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Referral</td><td>Payout per case</td><td class="rt">₹1,333</td><td class="rt" style="color:var(--set)">₹4,000</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Passing trade</td><td>Rent, signage, brand spend</td><td class="rt">₹951</td><td class="rt" style="color:var(--over)">₹29,000</td></tr>
  </table>

  <p><b>Read the table backwards.</b> Festive C3 produced the cheapest leads in the portfolio and not one car. The cheapest real customers came from the workshop, at ₹2,200. And showroom frontage, universally treated as free, cost ₹29,000 a booking.</p>

  <h3>Two numbers, never merged</h3>
  <p><b>Marketing cost per booking</b> is exact and unarguable. <b>Total cost per booking</b> adds salaries and rent and is directional, and every branch manager will argue about the allocation. They stay apart deliberately: the moment rent is allocated, the argument about allocation destroys the credibility of the first number, which was solid.</p>

  <h3>The three lead-level numbers</h3>
  <table>
    <tr><th>Name</th><th>Counts</th><th class="rt">A month</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Bookings</td><td>Leads that reached a booking</td><td class="rt">62</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Deals closed</td><td>Leads with at least one car delivered</td><td class="rt">51</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Cars delivered</td><td>Vehicles handed over</td><td class="rt">56</td></tr>
    <tr class="tot"><td>The delivery pipeline</td><td>Booked, no car delivered yet</td><td class="rt">11</td></tr>
  </table>
  <p>Cars exceed deals because one lead can deliver several vehicles. <b>A twelve-vehicle fleet order is one deal closed and twelve cars delivered</b>, and any screen treating the two as one number reports a fleet month as a retail collapse.</p>
</section>

<!-- 12 -->
<section id="s12">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 12</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>Roles and access</h2>
  <p class="lede2">Twenty-two seats. Three separate layers that are commonly confused.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Layer</th><th>The question</th><th>Rule</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Landing</b></td><td>Where does this person start?</td><td>Exactly one workspace, never a chooser</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Permission</b></td><td>What may they open?</td><td>Per screen, per role</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Scope</b></td><td>Which records within it?</td><td>Own · team · branch · brand · group</td></tr>
  </table>
  <p>A branch manager lands on his decisions screen and can still reach telecalling. <b>Landing is not permission.</b></p>

  <h3>Access levels</h3>
  <div class="grid">
    <div class="card"><h5>Full workspace · 17 seats</h5><p>Their own screens and their own day. Telecaller, sales, receptionist, team leader, F&amp;I, delivery, service advisor, service telecaller, workshop manager, insurance, used car evaluator, used car sales, fleet, driving school, branch head, principal, dealer admin.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Task queue · 4 seats</h5><p>One list, large rows, one button. RTO clerk, accessories, sales admin, pre-delivery check. <b>Not a lesser product. The right one.</b> A clerk who does one thing forty times a day will never open an eleven-item menu.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Read only · 3 seats</h5><p>Parts, marketing head, accounts.</p></div>
    <div class="card"><h5>Not this cycle</h5><p>Technician, who works from a printed job card. HR.</p></div>
  </div>

  <h3>Two rows that are never configurable</h3>
  <ul>
    <li><b>Salary and employee cost</b> is never visible below the dealer principal.</li>
    <li><b>Product margin and commission</b> are dealer-admin only. An insurance executive gets a ranked recommendation with reasons and no margin figure anywhere, because a purely margin-driven ranking always puts the priciest policy first and the executive loses the customer's trust within a month.</li>
  </ul>

  <h4>Advito's own access</h4>
  <p>Three separate surfaces, not one admin panel. Support can fix a dealer's configuration, sees phone numbers masked by default, and <b>cannot see a rupee of pricing</b>. Every entry is time-limited, reason-coded against a ticket, and <b>visible to the dealer in his own audit log.</b> A vendor who can enter a client's data silently should not be trusted with it.</p>
</section>

<!-- 13 -->
<section id="s13">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 13</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>Pricing and packaging</h2>
  <p class="lede2">A platform fee per brand plus a shared enquiry allowance. Unlimited users, unlimited rooftops.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Plan</th><th class="rt">Platform, monthly</th><th class="rt">Enquiries included</th><th class="rt">Overage</th><th>Typically</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Core</b></td><td class="rt">₹35,000</td><td class="rt">3,000</td><td class="rt">₹9</td><td>One brand, 1–2 rooftops</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Growth</b></td><td class="rt">₹75,000</td><td class="rt">8,000</td><td class="rt">₹8</td><td>Two brands, 3–5 rooftops</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Scale</b></td><td class="rt">₹1,40,000</td><td class="rt">20,000</td><td class="rt">₹6</td><td>Three or more brands</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Each additional brand</td><td class="rt">+₹18,000–60,000</td><td class="rt">shared</td><td class="rt">n/a</td><td>Allowance pools across brands</td></tr>
  </table>

  <p>Telephony and WhatsApp are passed through at <b>cost plus 15%</b>. Steady state works out at roughly <b>₹12,500 to ₹29,500 per rooftop per month.</b></p>

  <h3>Why priced on enquiries and not on seats</h3>
  <p>Per-seat pricing punishes exactly the behaviour the product needs. A dealer who is paying per head will not give the RTO clerk, the accessories desk or the pre-delivery inspector a login, <b>and those are the seats where the delivery promise actually breaks.</b> Charging per enquiry means the dealer's incentive is to put everybody on it, which is also our incentive.</p>

  <div class="note"><b>Plans are data, not code.</b> Changing a price never requires a deployment. Existing contracts are pinned to the version they signed, and negotiated rates above 20% need a second approval and are logged.</div>

  <h3>What we track that most vendors do not</h3>
  <p><b>Cost to serve, per dealer</b> covers messages, call minutes, transcription, lookups, storage and support hours. Without it we cannot tell which customers are worth having. One live example: a group on a 20% negotiated discount runs at <b>3% gross margin.</b> Nobody would have known.</p>
</section>

<!-- 14 -->
<section id="s14">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 14</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>Why a dealer buys, and why he keeps it</h2>

  <h3>The buying argument, in one table</h3>
  <table>
    <tr><th>He currently cannot</th><th>With Arth</th><th>Worth, per month</th></tr>
    <tr><td>Tell which enquiries were never called</td><td>Sees it daily with a rupee figure</td><td class="rt">₹39L exposed</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Tell which advertising sold a car</td><td>Cost per booking by creative</td><td class="rt">₹38k wasted spend found</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Tell why he loses</td><td>Controlled lost reasons, by competitor</td><td class="rt">41 customers to one rival</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Tell which promises broke</td><td>Promise accuracy, by branch and person</td><td class="rt">CSI score protected</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Tell which staff actually work hard</td><td>Difficulty-weighted scores</td><td class="rt">Best performer identified</td></tr>
  </table>

  <h3>Why he keeps it: the three that compound</h3>
  <ol class="n">
    <li><b>His history lives here.</b> After two years the customer records, service histories and attribution chains are the dealership's memory. Leaving means losing it.</li>
    <li><b>Manufacturer reporting stops being manual.</b> Five to eight hours a month of assembling figures from three systems that never quite agree, replaced by a generated report. Unglamorous, and it is the reason a general manager argues to keep the product.</li>
    <li><b>The advertising performs better.</b> Delivered cars fed back as conversion events improve the bidding. Cancelling Arth makes the same ad budget worse.</li>
  </ol>

  <div class="warn"><b>The churn signal to watch is adoption, not satisfaction.</b> A dealer whose service team has not logged in for nine days is not a support ticket, it is a cancellation in slow motion. Onboarding time is the best predictor we have: a group stalled at step three after four requests will not adopt.</div>
</section>

<!-- 15 -->
<section id="s15">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 15</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>Phases, and where we are</h2>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Phase</th><th>What it delivers</th><th>State</th></tr>
    <tr><td>1–3</td><td>Tenancy, org tree, positions, the ledger, the metrics engine</td><td><span class="pill p-ok">Complete</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td>4</td><td>Sales and telecalling workspaces. Click identifiers captured</td><td><span class="pill p-ok">Complete</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>5</b></td><td><b>Delivery chain first, then Service, Insurance, Used car, Accessories, Driving school</b></td><td><span class="pill p-mid">In construction</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td>6</td><td>Attribution and the money layer. Household</td><td><span class="pill p-mute">Scoped</span></td></tr>
    <tr><td>7</td><td>Exception Cockpit, manager cockpit, Advito three-surface split</td><td><span class="pill p-mute">Deferred by ruling</span></td></tr>
  </table>

  <h3>The honest position today</h3>
  <div class="stat">
    <div><div class="v">2 of 7</div><div class="l">Workspaces a dealer can use</div></div>
    <div><div class="v">80</div><div class="l">Screens specified</div></div>
    <div><div class="v">6</div><div class="l">Screens a person can open</div></div>
    <div><div class="v">~⅓</div><div class="l">Of the product a dealer would pay for</div></div>
  </div>
  <p><b>The specification is complete and the foundation is strong. The product is about a third built.</b> Those are both true and they are routinely confused: "93% of planned engineering" measures against the plan, not against a dealership's working day.</p>

  <h4>The two irreversible pieces</h4>
  <p>Working hours per branch, and the delivery promise as an append-only ledger. Everything else can be rebuilt if it is wrong. <b>Those two cannot</b>, and they gate most of what follows.</p>
</section>

<!-- 16 -->
<section id="s16">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 16</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>What we will never build</h2>
  <p class="lede2">Recorded so that each request is answered once rather than re-argued every quarter.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Not building</th><th>Because</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>A dealer management system</b></td><td>Manufacturer-mandated, five-year build, an incumbent the dealer cannot remove</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Accounting or payroll</b></td><td>Regulated, with statutory filings. We compute what is payable and export it</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Spare parts inventory</b></td><td>The DMS owns it. We show which jobs wait on which part, which the DMS cannot</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Body shop and insurance claims</b></td><td>A distinct workflow with distinct counterparties. A separate product if ever</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Telematics</b></td><td>Hardware, and the manufacturer owns the vehicle data</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Our own telephony or speech-to-text</b></td><td>Licensed businesses. We integrate</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>A native mobile app, this cycle</b></td><td>Responsive web avoids store review on every release and two codebases. Revisit when push or camera becomes essential</td></tr>
  </table>

  <div class="pull">The largest available scope error is building the thing a dealer already has, badly, alongside the thing nobody has, well.</div>
</section>

<!-- 17 -->
<section id="s17">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 17</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>Risks, honestly</h2>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Risk</th><th>Standing</th><th>What holds it</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Trademark unresolved</b><br>Classes 9 and 42</td><td><span class="pill p-no">Open</span></td>
      <td><b>Nothing.</b> The only risk on the programme with no mechanism, and its cost rises every week Phase 5 builds</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Bus factor</b><br>Single-person infrastructure, no successor</td><td><span class="pill p-no">Open</span></td>
      <td>Documented. Untested backups. A named second person is the fix</td></tr>
    <tr><td>No external penetration test</td><td><span class="pill p-mid">Deferred</span></td><td>Deferred with a named trigger: the second client</td></tr>
    <tr><td>No ISO 27001 or SOC 2</td><td><span class="pill p-mid">Deferred</span></td><td>Not required by the current segment. Required for enterprise groups</td></tr>
    <tr><td>No load or failure-mode testing at scale</td><td><span class="pill p-mid">Deferred</span></td><td>Scale thresholds instrumented in the deploy job</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Adoption, not features</td><td><span class="pill p-mid">Live</span></td><td>Onboarding time tracked as the churn predictor</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Moat is commercial, not technical</td><td><span class="pill p-mute">Structural</span></td><td>First-mover position and two years of dealer history</td></tr>
  </table>

  <div class="warn"><b>On the trademark.</b> Today an unavailable mark costs a brand book, a palette, a domain and two workspaces. After Phase 5 it costs seven workspaces, an eighty-screen prototype, whatever has been shown to a dealer principal, and the name on the signage. <b>It needs nothing that is not ready.</b></div>
</section>

<!-- 18 -->
<section id="s18">
  <div class="eyebrow">Chapter 18</div><div class="srule"></div>
  <h2>Vocabulary</h2>
  <p class="lede2">Words used precisely. Where two of these are used interchangeably, a number becomes wrong.</p>

  <table>
    <tr><th>Term</th><th>Means exactly</th></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Enquiry</b></td><td>One person's interest in one vehicle. The unit of work</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Booking</b></td><td>A lead that reached a booking. Counts <em>leads</em></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Deal closed</b></td><td>A lead with at least one car delivered. Counts <em>leads</em></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Cars delivered</b></td><td>Vehicles handed over. Counts <em>vehicles</em></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Parked</b></td><td>Latest disposition is postponed and the revisit date is future. <b>Derived, never stored</b></td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Difficulty band</b></td><td>Hot, warm, cold, very cold. Computed at assignment and frozen</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Expected value</b></td><td>(unit gross + attached gross) × stage probability. A ranking device first</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Promise accuracy</b></td><td>Delivered on or before the promise, excluding externally blocked chains</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Cost per booking</b></td><td>Marketing spend ÷ bookings. Never merged with total cost per booking</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Workspace</b></td><td>A department's day. Seven of them</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Seat</b></td><td>A person's role and their landing workspace. Twenty-two of them</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Position</b></td><td>A post in the org tree. Step owners and escalation targets are Positions, never Users</td></tr>
    <tr><td><b>Ledger</b></td><td>An append-only table with update and delete revoked at the database</td></tr>
  </table>
</section>

<footer>
  <b>Arth · The Product Book · Edition 01</b><br>

  Amendments in writing. Where this book and a working document disagree on product intent, this book governs; where they disagree on implementation, the Build Specification governs.
</footer>
